prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Mathematical Methods from the first year
Mastery of thermometry and calorimetry concepts
Application of the first and second principles to closed systems and simple thermodynamic cycles

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and aptitudes in the field of Mechanical Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Knowledge for carrying out measurements, calculations, valuations, appraisals, expert reports, studies, reports, work plans, and other similar tasks.
Ability to analyze and evaluate the social and environmental impact of technical solutions.
Ability to prevent occupational risks and protect the health and safety of workers and users.
Honesty, responsibility, ethical commitment, and a spirit of solidarity.
Ability to work in a team.
Acquire knowledge of applied thermodynamics and heat transfer: Basic principles and their application to solving engineering problems.
Relate the field of study of Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer and know the most important applications of both disciplines in the field of Thermal Engineering.
Apply mass, energy, and entropy balances to various systems, including the main equipment present in industrial plants (engines, turbines, compressors, boilers, condensers, etc.).

Understand the equipment that integrates power generation cycles (steam, gas, and combined) and refrigeration cycles commonly used in industry and be able to perform their thermodynamic analysis to assess their energy efficiency.
Understand the main characteristics and fundamental physical laws on which the three basic heat transfer mechanisms (conduction, convection, and radiation) are based.
Mathematically express the equations that describe heat transfer in a physical problem from fundamental balances (mass, momentum, and heat) and the laws on which the basic mechanisms are based.

syllabus_topics: Properties and Processes in Thermodynamic Systems

Basic Concepts: Units of measurement. Gases: ideal, real, and Van der Waals. Equations of state. Pure substance: phases and diagrams. State properties: determination using tables and/or equations of state.
Basic Principles of Thermodynamics
First Principle of Thermodynamics. Sign convention. Application to closed and open systems in steady state.
Second Principle of Thermodynamics. Entropy definition and applications. Entropy generation. Isentropic efficiency of equipment.
Thermal Machines
The thermal machine: types and efficiency. The Carnot cycle: thermal efficiency. Thermal machine cycles operating as engines: thermal efficiency.
Gas power cycles: analysis of the Brayton cycle.
Steam power cycles: analysis of the Rankine cycle. Combined cycle.
Continuous refrigeration production by vapor compression of a refrigerant: analysis of the inverse Rankine cycle. The heat pump and its analysis.
Fundamentals of Heat Transfer
Fundamental concepts, characteristics of basic heat transfer mechanisms, and basic laws.
Conduction
Simple geometries: plane, cylindrical, and spherical wall. Critical insulation radius.
Additional surfaces: concept, temperature field, efficiency, and dissipation coefficient. Heat transfer through finned surfaces.
Heat transfer in common configurations: shape factor in conduction.
Convection
Analysis methods in forced and natural convection.
Use of empirical correlations in forced and natural convection.
Radiation
Fundamentals of thermal radiation. Radiative properties. Black body and gray body. Heat transfer by radiation between two surfaces. Combined heat transfer mechanisms.
assessment_rules: For students with continuous evaluation, the final grade is calculated as (0.1 x PA) + (0.1 x PL) + (0.1 x TG) + (0.7 x EX), provided the written exam (EX) score is 3.5 or higher. If EX is less than 3.5, the final grade is the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. A final score of 5.0 or higher is required to pass the course. For students with differentiated evaluation, the final grade is (0.3 x EP) + (0.7 x EX), with the same minimum EX score of 3.5 and passing threshold of 5.0. In extraordinary calls, for students with continuous evaluation, the grade is based on (0.1 x PA) + (0.1 x PL) + (0.1 x TG) + (0.7 x EX) if EX is 3.5 or higher; otherwise, the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. For students with differentiated evaluation, the extraordinary call consists of a written exam (EX) and a practice exam (EP), with the same weighting and conditions as the ordinary call.
